title: WHO Says 45% of Dementia Cases Preventable, Adds Air Pollution as Risk Factor
excerpt: Updated guidelines identify 19 modifiable risk factors and advise against routine supplements, with particular urgency for India's 8.8 million dementia patients and its pollution crisis.
body:
• WHO's updated guidelines identify 19 modifiable risk factors and say up to 45% of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed
  • Air pollution is included for the first time as a population-level dementia risk factor — carrying major implications for India
  • The guidelines advise against routine use of vitamin B, vitamin E, omega-3, and multivitamin supplements for prevention
  • India has an estimated 8.8 million people aged 60 and above living with dementia, with cases expected to rise as the population ages

A Broader Net of Prevention

The World Health Organization on July 15 published the second edition of its guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia, expanding its framework from the original 2019 recommendations to cover 19 modifiable risk factors across four categories. The central finding: up to 45% of global dementia cases could be prevented or delayed through lifestyle changes, chronic disease management, and reducing environmental exposure.

"We know more today than ever before about what drives dementia risk, and these guidelines translate that knowledge into action. Countries now have clear, evidence-based recommendations they can put into practice immediately."

— Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General

Air Pollution Enters the Framework

The most consequential addition is air pollution, now formally recognized as a population-level dementia risk factor based on mounting evidence linking long-term exposure to polluted air with cognitive decline. For India — home to 21 of the world's 30 most polluted cities — the inclusion carries particular urgency.

A 2024 study published in BMJ Public Health had already identified both outdoor and indoor air pollution as important dementia risk factors among the Indian population. The WHO guidelines now provide a global policy basis for national action.

Other new risk factors added in this edition include HIV, stroke, traumatic brain injury, menopausal hormone therapy, sleep disorders, and vision impairment. The guidelines also introduce recommendations on multidomain interventions that target several risk factors simultaneously.

Supplements Get a Red Light

In a finding likely to challenge widely held assumptions, the WHO advised against the routine use of vitamins B and E, omega-3 fatty acids, and multivitamin-mineral supplements for dementia prevention in people without a diagnosed deficiency. Current evidence, the organization said, does not demonstrate sufficient benefit.

Instead, the guidelines recommend regular physical activity, tobacco cessation, limiting alcohol intake, healthy dietary patterns, social engagement, and mental stimulation. Effective management of hypertension, diabetes, and high cholesterol is also emphasized. For adults with hearing loss, the use of hearing aids received a new conditional recommendation for dementia risk reduction.

India's Growing Burden

Globally, 57 million people live with dementia, with over 60% in low- and middle-income countries. The condition costs the global economy an estimated $1.3 trillion annually — roughly half of which is unpaid care provided by family members and friends.

India faces a particularly acute challenge. A nationally representative study published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia estimated that approximately 8.8 million Indians aged 60 and above live with dementia, based on a prevalence rate of 7.4% among older adults. With India's elderly population projected to grow rapidly in the coming decades, public health experts say the WHO guidelines should serve as a catalyst for a coordinated national prevention strategy.

The updated recommendations arrive at a time when no widely accessible disease-modifying treatment or cure exists for dementia. Alzheimer's disease accounts for an estimated 60% to 70% of all cases. Prevention, the WHO emphasized, remains the most effective strategy — and the evidence base for acting on it has never been stronger.

For the Indian diaspora caring for aging parents across borders, the guidelines underscore the importance of addressing modifiable risk factors early — from managing chronic conditions to reducing pollution exposure — rather than relying on supplements marketed as cognitive protectors.
